r: Introduction to Linguistics builds beginning analytic skills across phonology, morphology, and syntax, plus comparative typology, acquisition, animal-communication contrasts, and language change, worked through mini-language problem sets rather than any single deliverable. These tasks map to Analyzing Data or Information and Processing Information, and task-exposure research finds science- and critical-thinking-heavy work like pattern-based linguistic problem solving negatively associated with AI exposure relative to writing or coding. General-purpose models can already solve many textbook phonology or morphology puzzles, but the course's instrumental purpose is training a novice's own analytic method on unfamiliar data, not producing a market-ready output AI could substitute for. No general-studies designation applies, so no transfer mandate binds the course; instead it is prerequisite substrate for four upper-division linguistics courses. At 24 months that foundational role, not institutional lock-in, keeps the instrumental need largely intact.

By 2031, AI systems will solve introductory phonology, morphology, and syntax problems fluently and could plausibly walk a student through the reasoning, narrowing the gap between the tool and the pedagogical exercise. Capability-trend evidence describing rapid growth in the length and difficulty of tasks models handle competently supports that expectation. Still, this course is foundational scaffolding: Morphology and Syntax, Phonetics, Phonetics and Phonology, and Phonology all require it as a prerequisite, and a program cannot let AI supply that substrate without reworking its entire upper-division sequence within one catalog cycle. The instrumental case erodes toward using AI as a check on one's own analysis rather than eliminating the analysis itself, capping the rating at Medium regardless of how competently a model solves the exercises. Diffusion data still show AI adoption uneven across instructional contexts at this horizon, moderating the pace of actual classroom substitution.

A decade out, the central case has AI solving essentially any bounded linguistic problem set posed in this course, and capability growth compounds enough that raw task automatability plausibly reaches the high band. Even so, the course's role as prerequisite substrate for the department's phonetics, phonology, and syntax sequence persists in the central case, because restructuring that chain would require deliberate curricular redesign rather than passive drift, and no accreditation or GT change is anticipated to force it. The instrumental need shifts from problem-solving execution toward building the conceptual vocabulary a student needs to follow and evaluate AI-assisted linguistic analysis in later coursework. The rating holds at Medium, capped by foundational role rather than by task-exposure, which by 2036 would otherwise justify High; genuine uncertainty remains about how much introductory problem-solving practice migrates to AI-assisted formats without eliminating the requirement.
LING 2010.d: Students learn the basic analytic skills to view language from a variety of perspectives in this course. In addition to studying language structure (phonology, morphology, and syntax), students discover how languages around the world differ from one another, how children acquire language, how animal communication is distinct from human language, how people use language as a form of social identity, and how languages change over time. Students solve mini-language problems and discuss the relevance of language to their daily lives throughout the course.

r: Origins of English Words traces the component parts of English vocabulary, tracks borrowings from languages such as German, Latin, French, Spanish, Greek, and Arabic, and builds transferable vocabulary and reading-comprehension tools rather than a specialized occupational skill. Etymology lookup and word-history explanation are tasks AI already performs fluently and with low error cost, since a wrong etymology is easily checked against reference sources, giving this course a lower verification burden than most in the catalog. It carries a bare General Studies: Arts and Humanities label with no GT code, which under the institutional-lock rule still counts as a real transfer mandate. At 24 months the instrumental need is only modestly eroded: the general-education requirement fixes the course in the curriculum regardless of how easily AI could supply the same etymological facts on demand.

By 2031, AI reference tools will answer etymology and word-formation questions instantly and reliably, and observed-usage patterns already show general knowledge-lookup tasks among the most heavily used consumer applications of these models. The applied task this course teaches, tracing word origins and morphological components to build vocabulary, is exactly the kind of low-verification-burden, fully digital lookup work that erodes fastest under sustained capability growth. What holds the rating from falling further is the General Studies designation: it remains a mandated transfer option within the Arts and Humanities area regardless of how automatable etymology becomes, and that mandate does not relax within a single catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting real erosion in the applied task offset by the institutional requirement that the course continue to exist and transfer.

Over a decade, AI etymology and vocabulary tools will be ubiquitous, cheap, and highly reliable, and the instrumental case for a dedicated course teaching word-origin lookup as a discrete skill weakens substantially in the central case. The general-education Arts and Humanities requirement is the binding constraint that keeps the rating from falling to Low: gtPathways-style transfer architecture changes through statutory and system-level processes, not through incremental technology adoption, and nothing in the current trajectory suggests that changing by 2036. The genuine uncertainty is whether the course's content shifts toward more defensible critical-thinking framing, such as semantic drift or cross-linguistic contact, to preserve pedagogical value even as its literal vocabulary-building function is largely absorbed by ambient AI tools. The rating holds Medium, capped by the transfer mandate rather than by task difficulty.
LING 2011.d: In this course, students study the component parts of English words and the way that speakers and writers create and change words and word meaning. Students consider why and when words are borrowed from other languages, such as German, Latin, French, Spanish, Greek, and Arabic. This course provides students with tools they can use to improve their vocabulary and reading comprehension throughout their lives. It is particularly valuable for students who plan to pursue careers in medicine, law, education, psychology, philosophy, culinary arts, and the humanities, and for all students who want to improve their language skills.

r: Analyzing English trains prospective English teachers to analyze the form of words and the structure of sentences in order to use the language more effectively in instructional settings, covering phonology, morphology, and syntax through a practical, applied lens. Structural parsing of English sentences and morphological analysis are tasks large language models already perform with real competence, since they were trained heavily on exactly this kind of formal linguistic pattern recognition, placing the course's core task closer to the analytical middle of the exposure spectrum than the protected critical-thinking end. There is no general-studies designation and no downstream linguistics course lists this as a prerequisite, so neither institutional lock-in nor foundational scaffolding caps the rating. At 24 months AI can already produce competent structural analyses of English text, though verifying pedagogical usefulness for classroom application still requires the instructor-in-training's own judgment.

By 2031, AI parsing and morphological-analysis tools will handle structural breakdowns of English text with high reliability across most everyday sentences, and observed-usage data continue to show language-analysis and writing-adjacent tasks among the largest categories of actual deployment. Real-deliverable benchmarking indicates models are approaching, though not yet matching, human-expert quality on applied language tasks of this kind, which supports a rising but not yet complete automatability. Because the course carries no general-studies designation and functions as a terminal rather than foundational component of the curriculum, no institutional cap holds the rating down. The instrumental case shifts toward Analyzing English becoming less necessary for producing correct structural analyses and more necessary for the pedagogical judgment of applying that analysis in a classroom, but the applied-task automatability itself supports a High rating at this horizon.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems performing structural analysis of English morphology and syntax reliably enough that the raw task this course drills is substantially automated, consistent with capability-trend evidence describing steadily lengthening and more difficult tasks models handle competently. Neither a general-studies mandate nor a foundational role protects the course from that erosion, since it sits outside gtPathways and nothing else in the catalog requires it as a prerequisite. The genuine uncertainty at ten years concerns how teacher-preparation programs adapt pedagogy once AI reliably performs the underlying linguistic analysis: the course's continued value likely shifts toward teaching prospective teachers to evaluate and correct AI-generated grammatical analysis for classroom use rather than to perform it unaided. The rating holds High, with real hedging about whether that instructional-application residue later warrants reassessment.
LING 3011.d: This course is a practical approach to English language structure (i.e. phonology, morphology, and syntax), particularly useful to prospective teachers of English. In this course students learn to analyze the form of English words and structure of English sentences with the goal of understanding how to use the language effectively. Students also gain a stronger understanding and appreciation of the linguistic diversity in today's society.

r: History of the English Language traces the internal history of English, including sound changes, inflectional loss, and syntactic shift, alongside the external political, social, and cultural forces that shaped its many varieties, synthesizing linguistic and historical evidence into a coherent narrative. Explaining documented sound changes and summarizing periods of English is a retrieval-and-synthesis task AI already performs competently, since it draws on well-documented, non-adversarial historical linguistic scholarship rather than live judgment calls. The course carries no general-studies designation and is not a listed prerequisite for other linguistics courses, so no institutional or foundational cap applies. At 24 months the instrumental need is still real because synthesizing internal and external historical factors into original analysis remains a meaningfully unautomated classroom exercise, even as factual retrieval is already largely AI-deliverable for the student who wants it.

By 2031, AI models will fluently synthesize the internal and external historical narratives this course covers, connecting sound change, morphological simplification, and syntactic development to the social and political history of English with a coherence approaching what the course currently teaches students to produce themselves. Diffusion data show firm-level AI adoption still uneven at this horizon, but classroom and study-tool adoption of historical-synthesis assistants is plausibly faster than firm-level averages given how well-suited the task is to retrieval-augmented generation. With no general-studies designation and no downstream prerequisite role protecting it, the course's applied task is substantially exposed. The rating rises to High, reflecting that the historical-linguistic synthesis this course trains is close to fully AI-deliverable well before the ten-year horizon, even though appreciation of the material for its own sake persists.

Over a decade, AI capability applied to historical-linguistic synthesis will very plausibly exceed what an undergraduate course can train a student to produce independently, per the trend of rapidly lengthening task-horizons models can handle competently. Nothing in the course's structure, neither a general-studies mandate nor a role as prerequisite substrate, caps that erosion, so the rating holds at High. The genuine uncertainty is not about capability but about whether the course's actual value migrates toward critical evaluation of AI-generated historical-linguistic claims, an activity task-exposure research suggests is more resistant, or whether the course itself becomes primarily an appreciation elective. Either way, the instrumental need for a student to personally perform the synthesis this course currently drills is credibly diminished by 2036 in the central case.
LING 3020.d: Students in this course study the linguistic, cognitive, and social factors that have combined to make the English language, in its many varieties, what it is today. These include factors from the internal history of English, such as sounds, inflections, and syntax, and the external history of English, such as political, social, and cultural influences.

r: Semantics studies meaning in natural language, examining how meaning develops, which linguistic units carry it, and how speakers use language to convey it, through the basic concepts, theories, and analytical techniques of contemporary semantic theory. This is a theory-heavy, abstract-reasoning course, and task-exposure research finds science- and critical-thinking-intensive work negatively associated with AI exposure relative to writing and routine analysis, which somewhat protects the course's core content even though AI can already discuss and apply semantic frameworks like compositionality or truth conditions competently. No general-studies designation applies, and the course sits outside any prerequisite chain to other linguistics courses, so neither institutional lock-in nor foundational scaffolding caps the rating. At 24 months AI assists with explaining semantic theories, but original application of those theories to new linguistic data still requires student-performed analysis.

By 2031, AI systems will apply major semantic frameworks, including compositional, formal, and cognitive approaches to meaning, to novel linguistic examples with real facility, since these are rule-governed analytical techniques similar in structure to the formal reasoning tasks models handle increasingly well per capability-trend evidence. The jagged-frontier finding that AI users perform worse when working outside a model's competence area is a genuine caution for semantic edge cases involving pragmatics or context-dependent meaning, where verification still benefits from expert judgment. With no general-studies mandate or foundational role protecting the course, the applied theoretical-analysis task is substantially exposed at this horizon. The rating rises to High: the theoretical technique itself becomes largely AI-deliverable, even though genuinely novel or contested semantic judgments retain some human-verification value.

A decade out, the central case has AI applying semantic theory to linguistic data as competently as an advanced undergraduate, extending the trend of models handling longer and more conceptually demanding tasks. No general-studies designation or foundational-scaffolding role caps the erosion, so the rating holds High. The meaningful hedge concerns genuinely contested or context-saturated meaning judgments, such as irony, novel metaphor, or culturally specific pragmatics, where the jagged-frontier problem persists and human interpretive judgment may retain real value even as routine semantic analysis is automated. Whether Semantics as a course shifts toward exactly that residue, or continues teaching techniques AI already performs, is not resolvable from the description alone, but the instrumental case for the current applied-analysis task is credibly diminished by 2036.
LING 3030.d: This course is the study of meaning in natural language. Students examine the development of meaning, the significant linguistic units that carry meaning, and the ways people use language to convey meaning. The course deals with basic concepts, theories, and analytical techniques in contemporary linguistics.

r: Morphology and Syntax is an intermediate study of English and comparative structure using structural linguistics and generative-transformational syntactic theory, requiring students to analyze language structures and engage the theoretical approaches behind them. Formal syntactic analysis, building phrase-structure or transformational derivations from data, is a rule-governed, symbolic task structurally similar to programming and formal logic, categories that task-exposure research classifies among the most AI-exposed rather than the most protected. LING 2010 is a prerequisite for this course, but nothing downstream depends on it, so it carries no foundational-scaffolding cap, and it has no general-studies designation. At 24 months AI already generates competent syntactic derivations for many English sentences, though applying generative-transformational theory correctly to genuinely novel or cross-linguistic data still commonly requires expert-guided practice.

By 2031, AI models will construct syntactic trees and morphological derivations across generative-transformational frameworks with high reliability, extending naturally from their existing strength on rule-governed symbolic tasks and consistent with observed usage data showing the Computer and Mathematical category as the largest share of actual model use. Because formal syntax is close in kind to programming and formal-logic tasks, the raw applied-task automatability at this horizon is substantial. No general-studies mandate or foundational role caps the rating, since the course is terminal within the linguistics sequence and outside gtPathways. The rating rises to High: the technical skill of producing correct syntactic and morphological analyses is largely AI-deliverable, even as instructors may still value the exercise for developing a student's own theoretical fluency.

A decade out, capability-trend evidence describing rapid growth in task length and difficulty models handle competently supports a central case where formal syntactic and morphological analysis is essentially solved for AI across the range of structures this course covers, comparable to how symbolic and programming tasks have automated. Nothing structural in the course, no general-studies designation and no downstream dependency, caps that erosion, so the rating holds High. The open question is pedagogical rather than technical: whether producing syntactic derivations by hand retains value as a way of internalizing generative-transformational theory even after AI can generate the same derivations instantly, a question this rating cannot resolve, though the instrumental case for the applied task itself is credibly high by 2036.
LING 3040.d: This is an intermediate study of syntax and morphology using basic principles of structural linguistics and generative- transformational syntactic theory. Although the course focuses on English, the structure of other languages is also covered. Both the analysis of language structures and the discussion of relevant theoretical approaches to those structures are involved.

r: This introductory course pairs language sounds, or phonetics, with sound systems, or phonology, emphasizing articulation while also covering acoustics and perception, and has students learn and apply the International Phonetic Alphabet to transcribe phonemes and conduct phonological analysis using distinctive features and rule formalism. IPA transcription and phonological rule application are partly perceptual, requiring the student to hear and discriminate speech sounds, which keeps some embodiment in the task even though the analytical write-up is digital. AI transcription and phonological-analysis tools already exist but are not yet reliably accurate across the range of world languages this course samples. No general-studies designation or downstream-dependency role caps the rating. At 24 months the instrumental need to build a student's own perceptual and analytical phonological skill remains largely intact.

By 2031, automatic phonetic transcription and computational phonological-rule tools will be considerably more accurate across diverse languages, extending the trend of models handling increasingly demanding perceptual-analytical tasks. Because the analytical half of the course, applying distinctive features and rule formalism to transcribed data, is fully digital and rule-governed, it is more exposed than the perceptual transcription-by-ear component, where the jagged-frontier problem cautions that AI transcription can be confidently wrong on unfamiliar phonemic inventories. With no general-studies mandate or foundational-scaffolding cap in play, the balance tips toward High: the course's applied analytical task is substantially AI-deliverable even though the perceptual-training component retains some protective value against full automation. Observed-usage data showing steady growth in technical-analytical AI use in education support this trajectory, and diffusion into standard phonetics curricula is plausible well before the ten-year horizon, though classroom adoption still lags raw model capability at this stage.

A decade out, computational phonetic and phonological tools will very plausibly handle transcription and rule-based analysis across most of the world's documented languages competently, consistent with rapid capability growth in perceptual and pattern-recognition tasks. Neither a general-studies designation nor a foundational role protects the course from that erosion, so the rating holds High. The genuine hedge is the perceptual-training function: learning to hear and discriminate speech sounds by ear may retain independent pedagogical value distinct from producing a correct transcription, and it is not obvious that AI substitutes for that trained perceptual competence even when it can output the same transcription. The instrumental case for the analytical task itself, however, is credibly high by 2036, and the jagged-frontier caution about confidently wrong AI transcriptions on unfamiliar phonemic inventories only partially tempers that conclusion, since the course's own language sample is broad but not exhaustive.
LING 3043.d: This course is an introductory study of language sounds (phonetics) and language sound systems (phonology), focusing primarily on the articulation of sounds, but also including discussion of acoustics and sound perception. The students will learn and practice using the International Phonetic Alphabet. Looking at various languages of the world, including English, the students will analyze the phonemes and conduct phonological analyses, using distinctive features and rule formalism.

r: Phonetics is an in-depth study of articulatory, acoustic, and auditory phonetics for majors and minors, requiring proficiency with the International Phonetic Alphabet, collecting acoustic speech data, and interpreting waveforms and spectrograms. Collecting speech data requires a human speaker and recording setup, and interpreting acoustic output involves perceptual pattern-recognition that AI tools handle unevenly outside well-documented phoneme sets, a jagged-frontier caution given how specialized and majors-focused this course's data is. LING 2010 is a prerequisite, and this course itself is prerequisite to LING 3045, giving it a moderate foundational role rather than a terminal one. There is no general-studies designation. At 24 months the instrumental need to build hands-on acoustic-analysis competence, including data collection, remains largely intact and is additionally protected at this horizon by its role feeding Phonology.

By 2031, spectrogram interpretation and acoustic-measurement software will be considerably more capable and widely used in phonetics instruction, and observed usage data show technical-analytical tasks are a substantial and growing share of actual AI deployment. Still, the data-collection component, recording live speech from human subjects, retains some embodiment, and the moderate foundational role of feeding LING 3045 caps any erosion at Medium specifically at the 24-month mark rather than restraining later horizons. By five years the applied analytical task of measuring and interpreting acoustic data is substantially automatable, and with the foundational cap not reaching this far out, the rating rises to High: the technical measurement and interpretation task is largely AI-deliverable even as data collection retains a residual human component.

A decade out, acoustic measurement and spectrogram interpretation will very plausibly be routine, reliable AI functions, extending the pattern of rapid capability growth in structured perceptual-analytical work. The course's moderate foundational role, as prerequisite to Phonology, only caps the rating at the 24-month horizon under the deterministic rule, so it does not restrain the ten-year rating. The most durable human residue is likely the physical act of eliciting and recording speech data from live subjects, an embodied task that acoustic-analysis software does not itself perform, but the analytical interpretation this course centers on is credibly high-automatable by 2036. The rating holds High, with genuine uncertainty about how much data-collection protocol remains a taught, hands-on skill and how much of the majors-level course shifts toward directing and validating AI-generated acoustic analysis rather than producing it manually from raw recordings.
LING 3044.d: This course, designed for Linguistics majors and minors, is an in-depth study of language sounds, how humans produce them, and how humans perceive them. Students learn about all three branches of the field: articulatory, acoustic, and auditory phonetics. Students also gain proficiency in using the International Phonetic Alphabet, collecting acoustic speech data, and interpreting waveforms and spectrograms.

r: Phonology is an in-depth study of sound systems and speech-sound patterning for majors and minors, using data from a broad sampling of world languages to analyze phonemic structures and conduct phonological analysis with distinctive features and rule formalism. This is formal, symbolic, rule-based analysis performed on already-transcribed data rather than live acoustic collection, placing it closer to the digital, pattern-governed tasks that current AI systems handle competently. LING 2010 and LING 3044 are prerequisites, but nothing downstream depends on this course itself, so it carries no foundational-scaffolding cap and no general-studies designation. At 24 months AI can already propose plausible rule-based analyses for many phonological patterns, though correctly analyzing typologically unusual or under-documented language data still commonly benefits from expert-guided instruction.

By 2031, AI systems will apply distinctive-feature theory and rule formalism to phonological data with high reliability across the well-documented language sample this course typically draws on, consistent with observed usage data showing the Computer and Mathematical category as the largest share of actual model use for structured symbolic work. Because the course is terminal, nothing in the linguistics sequence depends on it, and carries no general-studies mandate, no institutional cap restrains the rating. The instrumental case shifts toward High: producing a correct phonological analysis of a given dataset is a task AI increasingly performs on par with an advanced student, even as instructors may retain the exercise for its role in building theoretical fluency. Capability-trend evidence on lengthening task-horizons supports this shift continuing rather than plateauing, and diffusion into standard linguistics coursework is plausible within this window even though firm-level AI adoption more broadly remains uneven.

A decade out, capability-trend evidence pointing to models handling longer and more difficult structured-reasoning tasks supports a central case where phonological rule analysis across most of the world's documented languages is reliably AI-performed, similar to the trajectory expected for syntactic analysis. No general-studies designation or downstream dependency protects the course from that erosion, so the rating holds High. The genuine hedge concerns typologically rare or sparsely documented languages, where limited training data could keep AI phonological analysis less reliable and the jagged-frontier risk of confident errors more salient, preserving some role for expert human judgment. For the well-documented core of the course's content, though, the instrumental case for the applied task is credibly high by 2036, and the course's practical value likely migrates toward evaluating and correcting AI-proposed phonological analyses rather than deriving them entirely by hand.
LING 3045.d: This course is designed for Linguistics majors and minors. In this course, students engage in an in-depth study of language sound systems and patterning of speech sounds. Using data from a broad sampling of the world's languages, as well as from English, students learn to analyze phonemic structures and conduct phonological analysis using distinctive features and rule formalism.

r: Language and Society examines how social context shapes speech, covering language variation, dialects, pidgins and creoles, bilingualism, linguistic solidarity and politeness, and language planning, with field methods and ethical research procedures integral to the course. The analytical half, categorizing variation patterns and applying sociolinguistic frameworks, is a digital, text-based task AI performs reasonably well, while the field-methods component requires real-time interaction with human informants and ethical judgment calls that are more resistant to substitution. No general-studies designation applies, and the course is terminal with no downstream dependency, so neither institutional lock-in nor foundational scaffolding caps the rating. At 24 months the instrumental need remains largely intact because the fieldwork-and-ethics component anchors a meaningful part of the course in embodied, human-judgment-dependent practice.

By 2031, AI tools will competently apply sociolinguistic frameworks to describe and categorize language-variation patterns from transcribed or documented data, extending the trend of rising task-exposure in text-based analytical work. But eliciting speech from real informants under ethical research protocols, building the rapport fieldwork requires, and making live judgment calls about consent and representation remain interpersonal, presence-dependent tasks that task-exposure research treats as comparatively protected. With no general-studies mandate or foundational role in play, the analytical component alone would justify a higher rating, but the fieldwork core keeps the overall applied-task picture mixed. The rating rises to High as the analytical share of the work becomes substantially AI-deliverable, while the fieldwork residue is flagged for closer scrutiny at the next horizon.

A decade out, sociolinguistic pattern analysis will very plausibly be a routine AI capability, but the field-methods and ethical-research component this course explicitly requires involves live human interaction whose verification burden rises rather than falls as AI mediates more of the surrounding analysis: an informant relationship or a consent judgment cannot be delegated to a model, and getting it wrong has real research-ethics consequences that are often non-obvious in the moment. That elevated verification burden triggers a downward adjustment from the trajectory the analytical task alone would suggest. The rating settles at Medium, reflecting substantial automation of the descriptive-analytical work alongside a persistently human-anchored fieldwork core; the balance between those two halves of the course is the central uncertainty at this horizon.
LING 3050.d: This course examines the dynamic relationships between language and society. The students will investigate why people speak differently in different social contexts by identifying the social functions of language and the ways in which language is used to convey social meaning. The course focuses on language variation, including such topics as languages and dialects, pidgins and creoles, bilingualism and multilingualism, linguistic solidarity and politeness, language planning and language change. Field methods, including ethical research procedures, are an integral part of the course.

r: This course applies linguistic method to legal language: parsing ambiguity in statutes and contracts, analyzing speech acts and metaphor in legal reasoning, and conducting forensic linguistic analysis of disputed authorship and recorded speech as evidence. These tasks map to interpreting information for others and evaluating evidence against legal standards. Text and pattern analysis of this kind sits inside AI's current competence, and observed-usage data shows writing and analytical tasks are heavily used already. But forensic linguistic conclusions function as expert testimony in an adversarial legal system, where a wrong attribution has direct consequences for a defendant and errors are contested by opposing counsel rather than self-evident. That verification burden binds at 24 months: the instrumental need for a human trained in forensic method is not eroded by AI's ability to draft comparable-looking analysis.

By 2031, AI tools for stylometric comparison, ambiguity detection, and drafting legal-linguistic analysis will be considerably more capable and likely embedded in litigation-support workflows, raising the base rate of automatable task performance. Observed-usage data already places computer-and-analytical work as the largest usage category, and that trend plausibly extends into legal-text analysis. Yet the jagged-frontier finding is directly on point here: outside a system's reliable competence, users relying on AI conclusions are measurably less accurate, and courts require conclusions that survive cross-examination by a human expert who understands the method's limits. That verification demand keeps a trained analyst necessary even as drafting and pattern-matching automate. The course's instrumental case rises to Medium as execution shifts toward AI while judgment and testimony remain human-anchored.

Over a decade, capability trend data suggests forensic text analysis tools will handle authorship attribution and ambiguity flagging with high nominal accuracy, and adoption in legal practice will likely be substantially wider than today, even given the diffusion evidence that firm-level AI use still lags capability. Still, the adversarial structure of the courtroom is an institutional feature, not a capability gap: expert findings must be defensible under scrutiny, and a system whose failure modes are non-obvious cannot itself hold that accountability. The central-case rating holds at Medium rather than rising further, because the binding constraint is verification and legal accountability rather than raw task difficulty. The genuine uncertainty is how much routine comparison automates, not whether courtroom-grade linguistic judgment remains a human role by 2036.
LING 3055.d: The use of language in the US legal system is analyzed from both theoretical and practical perspectives. On a theoretical level, issues related to the determination of meaning in legal language are studied, including ambiguity in interpreting laws (court decisions, statutes, and codes) and contracts, and the use of speech acts and legal fictions like metaphor to conceptualize meaning. On a practical level, the course introduces students to forensic linguistics, or the use of language as legal evidence. Forensic linguistics topics include both the use of written language as evidence of authorship (e.g., ransom notes, wills, etc.) and spoken language as evidence of identity (e.g., telephone threats, recorded conversations, etc.).

r: Students here analyze cross-linguistic typology and then apply that pattern knowledge to construct an original language: designing phoneme inventories, phonological rules, morphological systems, and syntax. This is fundamentally a digital, text-based synthesis task, close to the writing and structured-generation activities that observed-usage data identifies as the largest category of current AI use, and current models can already generate plausible phonological and grammatical systems on request. There is no licensure lock, no embodied component, and no high-stakes verification requirement; a flawed conlang carries no real-world error cost. At 24 months, AI is already a competent collaborator for much of the generative work the course assigns, though course adoption of these tools in assessed individual projects is still uneven, holding the rating at Medium rather than higher.

By 2031, language models will fluently generate internally consistent phonologies, morphologies, and syntactic systems on demand, and diffusion of such tools into student workflows is highly plausible given how directly conlanging resembles rule-governed creative writing, an activity task-exposure research ranks among the most exposed. Verification burden is minimal here: there is no adversarial stakeholder and no expert check required to catch a design that simply reflects the student's own choices, so the protective dampener does not apply. Embodiment is entirely absent since the work is symbolic and digital throughout. With no institutional lock-in and no foundational role for later required coursework, the instrumental case shifts to High: AI can perform the applied task competently, and little in the course's structure resists that.

A decade out, capability-trend evidence points toward AI systems handling elaborate constructed-language design, including internally consistent diachronic change and writing-system development, essentially on request. Nothing about this course's task profile changes that trajectory: it has no licensure or accreditation anchor, no embodied requirement, and no role as a prerequisite for other required courses, so none of the protective caps apply. The wide uncertainty band that governs labor-market claims elsewhere in this rubric matters less here, because the question is narrowly whether AI can perform the applied task the course teaches, not whether conlanging remains a valued creative pursuit. On that narrower question the central case is High: the instrumental rationale for students to build these systems unaided is substantially eroded by 2036.
LING 3065.d: In this course, students explore the nature of language through an analysis of constructed languages, including Esperanto, Modern Hebrew, Klingon, Dothraki, Na'vi, Quenya, and others. By the end of the course, students will have developed their own constructed languages, guided by rigorous study of the typology of patterns observed in real human languages. Topics covered include phoneme inventories, phonological rules, morphological classification, syntactic structure, language change over time, dialectal variation, and writing systems.

r: The applied work is philological: translating Old English texts using grammar and reference materials, parsing inflectional morphology, and situating passages in historical and cultural context. Translation sits explicitly among the most-exposed occupations in task-exposure research, and general-purpose models already produce serviceable renderings of Old English drawing on digitized corpora and grammars, though coverage and reliability for this lower-resource historical language remain more uneven than for major modern languages. That gap between raw capability and dependable, deployed competence keeps the 24-month rating from rising further. There is no licensure lock and no embodied requirement; the binding constraint is simply that adoption of AI for this specific historical-language task has not yet caught up to what general translation tools do for living languages.

By 2031, models trained on richer historical-language corpora will plausibly close much of the reliability gap that limits Old English translation today, and productivity research on AI-assisted writing and translation more broadly shows large speed and quality gains once a tool is trustworthy in its domain. Verification burden is moderate rather than protective here: a mistranslated passage is an academic error, not a safety or legal one, so scholarly review rather than expert gatekeeping suffices. Embodiment is absent, and the course carries no general-studies designation and is not a prerequisite for further required coursework, so no structural cap applies. The instrumental case for a student to develop this translation competence unaided weakens substantially, moving the rating to High even though the language's smaller corpus keeps some uncertainty around how completely automation displaces manual parsing.

Given the capability trend of doubling task-time horizons roughly every several months, a decade is ample for AI systems to handle historical-language translation, including Old English, with the same fluency seen for modern languages today. Nothing in the course's structure resists that: it has no licensure or accreditation anchor, no embodied component, and no gatekeeping role for later required courses, so the deterministic caps that protect foundational or mandated courses elsewhere do not apply here. The reasonable hedge is about how the field responds pedagogically, not about the technical trajectory. In the central case, the instrumental rationale for hand-translating Old English as a standalone skill is substantially eroded by 2036, holding the rating at High with real but secondary uncertainty about corpus and tooling maturity.
LING 3070.d: This course covers the basic vocabulary and grammar needed to read texts in Old English with the aid of reference materials. The grammatical structure of the language is studied in detail. The course also addresses the relevant cultural and historical contexts necessary for understanding Old English texts.

r: This course teaches reading Latin through vocabulary, grammar, and cultural context, with translation as the central applied task. Unlike lower-resource historical languages, Latin has decades of machine-translation development behind it and an enormous digitized corpus, so current AI tools already translate Latin passages with real fluency and are widely and actually used by students for exactly this purpose. Task-exposure research places translation among the most-exposed activities of any occupation category, and that finding transfers cleanly here. There is no licensure lock, no embodied requirement, and no general-studies designation capping the course. Because both AI competence and actual deployment are already high for Latin translation specifically, the 24-month rating starts at High rather than the Medium seen for less-resourced historical languages.

By 2031, Latin-capable translation and grammatical-analysis tools will be more deeply integrated into study workflows, and the productivity evidence for AI-assisted language work, including large measured speed gains on comparable text-heavy tasks, points toward even routine adoption in coursework. Verification burden is moderate, not protective: mistranslating a Latin passage is an academic error with low real-world cost, easily caught through the same instructor review already built into the course. Embodiment is entirely absent, and neither a general-studies designation nor a prerequisite role for later required courses constrains the rating. With capability and deployment both already strong and rising, the instrumental case for students to translate unaided continues to erode, holding the rating at High and leaving little room for a lower band even under conservative adoption assumptions.

A decade out, capability-trend evidence indicates AI translation of well-resourced classical languages will be effectively solved for practical purposes, and Latin, with its unusually large training corpus among historical languages, is a central case rather than an edge case for that trajectory. No institutional lock-in, embodied requirement, or foundational role for other required courses tempers the rating, so none of the deterministic caps engage. The genuine uncertainty concerns how classics programs reorient pedagogy toward interpretation, textual criticism, and cultural context rather than mechanical translation, not whether the translation task itself remains instrumentally necessary. In the central case that instrumental necessity is largely gone by 2036, and the rating remains High with confidence tempered only by how the discipline itself chooses to redefine what the course teaches.
LING 3075.d: This course covers the basic vocabulary and grammar needed to read texts in Latin with the aid of reference materials. The grammatical structure of the language is studied in detail. The course also addresses the relevant cultural and historical contexts necessary for understanding Latin texts.

r: This variable-topics course rotates across subfields such as conversation analysis, applied linguistics, and advanced syntax, built around individualized student projects rather than a fixed task set. That breadth makes the applied work harder to pin to a single occupational activity, but most plausible subtopics reduce to analyzing linguistic data and documenting findings in writing, activities that observed-usage data shows are already heavily used with AI assistance. There is no general-studies designation and no licensure anchor, and the analytical work is entirely digital. At 24 months, AI already assists meaningfully with the data analysis and drafting components of an individualized project, though the syllabus's topic-dependent nature and the instructor-guided originality expected of the project moderate how much any single offering is actually automated in practice.

By 2031, whichever subtopic a given offering covers, AI tools for corpus search, discourse annotation, and stylistic analysis will be considerably more capable, and the same productivity gains documented for professional writing and analytical tasks plausibly extend to individualized linguistics projects. Verification burden stays moderate: an instructor grading an independent project can catch analytical errors without expert-level adversarial scrutiny, so no dampener applies. The course carries no institutional lock-in and functions as an elective rather than scaffolding for further required coursework, so no cap holds the rating down. The instrumental case shifts to High, though confidence stays lower than for fixed-content courses because the description spans multiple task types that could diverge in exposure depending on which subfield a given semester happens to emphasize.

Over a decade, general capability growth should make AI a highly competent collaborator across whichever linguistic subfield a given topics offering addresses, from corpus-based conversation analysis to formal syntactic argumentation. Because the course carries no general-studies designation, no licensure anchor, and no foundational role feeding later required courses, none of the deterministic caps intervene, and the rating tracks the rising base rate directly to High. The central uncertainty here is less about AI capability, which the broader evidence base treats as likely to keep advancing quickly, and more about which specific subtopic a future section covers, since the variable-topics format means this rating represents an average across genuinely different possible course instances rather than one fixed, stable task the way a conventionally titled course would present.
LING 3080.d: The different topics within linguistics, some theoretical and some applied, range from conversation analysis to applied linguistics to stylistics to advanced syntax. Individualized projects are required. Students may repeat the course under different subtitles, up to a limit of 9 credit hours.

r: The applied work spans decipherment methodology, epigraphic analysis, and the cultural and sociopolitical history of writing systems from Mayan glyphs to runes, including an in-depth case study of Classic Mayan script. Comparative script analysis and expository writing about it are tasks AI already handles reasonably well, consistent with observed-usage data showing analytical and writing tasks as heavily used. But the course carries a General Studies: Arts and Humanities, Global Diversity designation, which under the gtPathways transfer framework is a binding institutional mandate regardless of how automatable the underlying content is. That designation caps the 24-month rating at Low outright: the course must exist and transfer within the general-education core, so the instrumental need for a student to take it is preserved by policy independent of AI capability.

By 2031, AI tools will more capably support decipherment reasoning, script comparison, and analytical writing about writing systems, and the underlying task-exposure of that written analytical work continues to rise, consistent with productivity research showing substantial gains on professional writing tasks. That would ordinarily push the rating toward High, but the gtPathways general-education designation caps any general-studies-designated course at Medium by the five-year horizon regardless of the base automatability score, since the statutory transfer core does not restructure on a single catalog cycle. The instrumental case therefore shifts from Low to Medium: the applied analytical work is increasingly AI-assisted, but the requirement that a student complete a transferable arts-and-humanities course persists as the binding constraint, independent of how well AI performs the decipherment and analysis tasks the course actually teaches.

A decade out, AI systems will plausibly be strong collaborators in epigraphic and comparative script analysis, and diffusion of such tools into humanities instruction is a reasonable central-case expectation even given the broader evidence that firm-level AI adoption still lags raw capability. Even so, the gtPathways general-education mandate is a statutory transfer requirement, not a discretionary curricular choice, and nothing in the capability trajectory changes that structure within this horizon. The rating holds at Medium, capped by institutional lock-in rather than by task difficulty. The honest uncertainty concerns how the course's content and assessment adapt to AI-assisted decipherment tools, not whether the general-education requirement itself persists through 2036, which the central case treats as essentially settled given how slowly statutory transfer frameworks tend to move.
LING 3090.d: From columns of Classic Mayan glyphs and Chinese characters to strings of Greek letters and Viking runes, the world's writing systems and scribal traditions are vast and diverse. In exploring this topic, the course examines how sounds, words, social meanings, and other properties of human languages are graphically adapted and culturally transformed into writing systems. Specific areas of focus include the historical development of writing systems, epigraphy and the decipherment of ancient languages, scribal artistry and craft, and the relationship between writing and sociopolitical power. Although surveying several writing systems and associated phenomena, the course also features an in-depth exploration of Classic Mayan writing (or another visually complex system).

r: Like its lower-numbered counterpart, this variable-topics course bridges linguistics with other disciplines through individualized interdisciplinary projects rather than a single fixed task. Most plausible offerings still reduce to gathering and analyzing linguistic data and producing written argumentation, activities that observed-usage data identifies as heavily represented in current AI use. There is no general-studies designation and no licensure anchor, and the work is entirely digital with no embodied component. At 24 months, AI already assists meaningfully with the analytical and drafting portions of an individualized interdisciplinary project, but the junior-standing prerequisite and the instructor-directed originality requirement mean actual classroom adoption of AI for the substantive intellectual work remains partial, holding the rating at Medium rather than higher despite the underlying task categories skewing toward what current tools already do competently.

By 2031, AI research and analysis tools will be considerably more capable at synthesizing cross-disciplinary linguistic material, and the productivity evidence for AI-assisted analytical writing plausibly extends to interdisciplinary independent projects of the kind this course requires. Verification burden remains moderate rather than protective: an instructor evaluating an individual project can catch flawed reasoning without expert adversarial review, so no dampener applies. The course carries no institutional lock-in and is not a prerequisite for further required coursework, so no structural cap holds the rating down. The instrumental case rises to High, with confidence tempered by the format's inherent variability across different interdisciplinary pairings from one offering to the next, which makes any single point estimate somewhat approximate rather than a precise forecast.

Over a decade, general-purpose capability growth should make AI a strong collaborator across whatever interdisciplinary pairing a given topics offering explores, whether linguistics meets anthropology, psychology, or computer science. No general-studies designation, licensure anchor, or foundational role in the required sequence constrains the course, so none of the deterministic caps intervene and the rating tracks the rising base rate to High. As with LING 3080, the residual uncertainty is less about the trajectory of AI capability, which the broader evidence base treats as likely to keep compounding, and more about which specific interdisciplinary topic a future section addresses, since this rating necessarily averages across variable course content that a fixed syllabus would not present to a rater, and different pairings could plausibly land on either side of the High threshold.
LING 4010.d: The different topics, some theoretical and some applied, are interdisciplinary and are designed to help the linguist bridge the gap between linguistics and various other disciplines. Individualized projects are required. Students may repeat the course under different subtitles, up to a limit of 9 credit hours. Any single variable topic may be used as an elective under either the linguistic or the interdisciplinary requirement, but not both.

r: The applied work is comparative: examining language data from many cultures and societies to identify structural variation and similarity, framed through the goals and methods of the anthropological linguist. This is analytical pattern-finding across datasets, a task AI already performs competently on digitized language data, though task-exposure research finds that science and critical-thinking-heavy work is comparatively less exposed than routine writing, which moderates the pace of substitution. There is no general-studies designation and no licensure anchor. At 24 months, AI meaningfully assists with data gathering and comparative summarization for the individualized projects the course requires, but the cultural-interpretive judgment central to anthropological analysis is not yet reliably automated at deployed scale, holding the rating at Medium rather than letting the exposed data-processing component alone carry the score higher at this early horizon.

By 2031, AI tools for cross-linguistic data analysis and comparative summarization will be considerably more capable, consistent with the broad capability-trend evidence of fast-doubling task-time horizons, and observed-usage patterns suggest such analytical tasks will see growing adoption. Verification burden is moderate rather than protective: an instructor can evaluate a comparative-linguistics project's reasoning without expert adversarial scrutiny, so no dampener applies. The course carries no institutional lock-in and is not prerequisite scaffolding for further required coursework, so no structural cap holds it down. The instrumental case shifts to High as AI increasingly performs the comparative data work, even as the anthropological framing of that data remains a partly human interpretive act that resists full automation on this horizon and across the horizon that follows.

A decade out, capability growth should make AI systems strong collaborators in cross-linguistic comparative analysis, surfacing structural patterns across large multilingual datasets with facility. Nothing in the course's structure resists that: no general-studies designation, no licensure anchor, and no gatekeeping role for other required courses, so none of the deterministic caps apply and the rating follows the rising base rate to High. The genuine uncertainty is less about whether AI can process comparative language data, which the capability trajectory makes likely, and more about whether the anthropological interpretation of that data continues to require a trained human framing it, a question this rubric's task-exposure evidence does not fully resolve looking out to 2036 and beyond that horizon, leaving the High rating a central estimate rather than a certainty.
LING 4011.d: This course analyzes the origins of language, its development, the similarities and the differences between natural languages in the context of various cultures and societies. The focus is on the goals, tasks, and methods of the anthropological linguist studying the language of a foreign culture. The class will examine data from a variety of languages in order to gain an awareness of the variation and similarities that exist in language structures around the world. Individualized projects are required. This course may be used as an elective to satisfy either the linguistic or the interdisciplinary requirement for the Linguistics major, but not both.

r: This course covers language families, sound change, and the comparative method used to classify languages historically. The applied task is pattern-based reconstruction: identifying regular sound correspondences and structural change across related languages, a systematic form of data analysis that AI tools already handle with reasonable competence on digitized comparative datasets. Task-exposure research finds critical-thinking and classification-heavy work comparatively less exposed than routine writing, which tempers the pace here relative to purely generative tasks. There is no general-studies designation and no licensure anchor, and the work is entirely digital. At 24 months, AI assists meaningfully with cognate identification and comparative summarization, but the scholarly judgment required for defensible language classification is not yet fully deployed at scale, keeping the rating at Medium.

By 2031, AI tools for computational historical linguistics, including automated cognate detection and phylogenetic language classification, will be considerably more capable and more available to students, consistent with the fast capability-trend growth documented across reasoning tasks generally. Verification burden remains moderate rather than protective: an instructor can assess a historical-linguistics argument without adversarial expert review, so no dampener applies. The course carries no institutional lock-in and does not scaffold further required coursework, so no structural cap holds the rating down. The instrumental case shifts to High as the comparative-method mechanics increasingly automate, even as the discipline's classificatory judgments retain some contested, expert-dependent character that keeps a fully mechanical reading of the rating from being appropriate at this stage of tool maturity.

A decade out, computational approaches to historical linguistics should be well embedded in the field, with AI systems performing much of the pattern-detection and classification work that once required painstaking manual comparison. No general-studies designation, licensure anchor, or foundational role in the required sequence constrains this course, so the deterministic caps do not engage and the rating follows the rising base rate to High. The honest hedge concerns how much of language classification remains genuinely contested and thus reliant on expert historical-linguistic judgment versus how much becomes a solved computational problem; the central case leans toward the latter by 2036, but the uncertainty is real and worth stating plainly rather than papering over it with a confident point estimate that the evidence does not fully support.
LING 4012.d: This course covers the various languages and language families of the world from an historical perspective. The student will study language change, methods of historical linguistics research, and language classification. Individualized projects are required. This course may be used as an elective to satisfy either the linguistic or the interdisciplinary requirement for the Linguistics major, but not both.

r: The course examines how language develops in monolingual and bilingual children and adults across phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics, and how language is used interactionally between parents and children, among peers, and across dialects. The applied work is interpreting acquisition data and explaining structural and interactional patterns, tasks that blend AI-competent literature synthesis with genuinely interpretive judgment about cognitive and interactional evidence. Task-exposure research finds science-adjacent critical-thinking work comparatively less exposed than routine writing, which moderates the 24-month rating. There is no general-studies designation and no licensure anchor. At 24 months, AI assists meaningfully with summarizing acquisition research and structural analysis for the course's individualized projects, but does not yet substitute for the interpretive core, holding the rating at Medium.

By 2031, AI tools for analyzing acquisition data, transcribing and coding child-adult interaction, and synthesizing psycholinguistic literature will be considerably more capable, consistent with fast capability-trend growth and with observed-usage patterns showing heavy uptake of analytical and writing assistance. Verification burden is moderate rather than protective: an instructor can evaluate an acquisition-focused project without adversarial expert review, so no dampener applies. The course carries no institutional lock-in and is not prerequisite scaffolding for further required coursework, so no structural cap holds the rating down. The instrumental case shifts to High as data processing and literature synthesis increasingly automate, even as the interactional data itself still originates from real caregiver-child and peer exchanges that a model can analyze but did not itself generate or observe.

A decade out, AI systems should be strong collaborators in psycholinguistic analysis, capable of coding interaction transcripts, modeling acquisition trajectories, and synthesizing cross-linguistic developmental evidence with real sophistication. No general-studies designation, licensure anchor, or foundational role for other required courses constrains this course, so the deterministic caps do not engage and the rating follows the rising base rate to High. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much of the interpretive work connecting acquisition data to cognitive theory remains a distinctly human judgment versus becomes AI-assisted synthesis; the central case leans toward substantial automation of the analytical work by 2036, with real but secondary uncertainty about the pace of that shift and about how much interactional data collection itself stays a human-run activity.
LING 4013.d: This course examines language development in monolinguals as well as bilingualism/multilingualism in children and adults. It covers all levels of language structure (phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics) and language use (linguistic interactions between parents and children, among children themselves, and between speakers across dialects). Individualized projects are required. This course may be used as an elective to satisfy either the linguistic or the interdisciplinary requirement of the Linguistics major, but not both.

r: Translation Studies applies theories of equivalence and cultural mediation to the practical task of rendering texts across languages, and introduces translation-memory and CAT software, work mapping onto O*NET's Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others and Translating Information into a Format Others Can Use. Task-exposure research explicitly classifies translators and interpreters among the most-exposed occupations, and observed-usage data shows writing and language tasks already form a prominent share of consumer and API activity. Commercial neural and generative machine translation already handles routine multilingual text competently, so the raw translation task is realized-automatable now, not merely capable. What the course still protects is judgment over the cultural, ideological, and philosophical dimensions the description foregrounds -- connotation, ethical framing, genre appropriateness -- where machine output still misjudges nuance. With no general-studies designation or licensure mandate, the binding constraint at 24 months is this qualitative verification burden rather than institutional lock-in, holding the rating at Medium rather than High.

By 2031, diffusion data suggests AI translation tools will be embedded in more workflows even though firm-level adoption still lags capability, and productivity research on professional writing -- large time savings paired with quality gains -- plausibly extends to translation drafting and post-editing. The instrumental case for hand-translating routine text erodes further, pushing the course toward teaching post-editing, quality assessment, and the theoretical vocabulary needed to specify what 'faithful' translation means for a given genre. Verification burden remains real: the jagged-frontier finding that users misjudge AI output outside its competence zone is acute in literary, legal, and diplomatic translation, where a fluent but culturally wrong rendering is a non-obvious failure. No general-studies or licensure lock exists to cap the rating institutionally, so the base automatability climb from realized capability and adoption pushes this to High, tempered only by genuine uncertainty about how fast literary and high-context translation follows general text.

Ten years out, sustained capability growth on the METR/Epoch trend and continued diffusion make it plausible that AI systems perform the large majority of translation tasks this course currently trains students to do by hand, including much of the culturally sensitive judgment that currently anchors the Medium-to-High case. The course's likely surviving function is training translators as expert reviewers and specifiers of machine output for high-stakes genres, plus theoretical literacy about translation as a discipline -- valuable but no longer instrumentally load-bearing for most translation work itself. This is a genuinely wide-uncertainty horizon: whether literary and diplomatic translation retains meaningful human-only demand depends on adoption patterns and client trust that are not yet observable. Absent any general-studies or licensure floor, nothing structurally protects the rating from reaching High, and the central case, hedged, places it there rather than assuming continued human necessity.
LING 4016.d: The course provides a comprehensive coverage of the major theories of translation. Both theoretical and practical aspects of translation are discussed in detail. Students analyze numerous case studies and perform translation considering the many cultural, ideological, ethical, and philosophical aspects of texts of various genres. Students are introduced to translation memory and software.

r: Modern Language Theory has students apply typological classification and at least one in-depth theoretical framework to analyze unfamiliar linguistic structures, plus prepare job-search materials -- work mapping to O*NET's Analyzing Data or Information and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others. Task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking-intensive tasks are negatively associated with exposure, which argues against overstating automatability of novel linguistic analysis, yet observed-usage data shows the Computer & Mathematical category, which includes formal analytical work, is already the largest usage share. Applying a known typological or generative framework to new data is a bounded reasoning task current models handle with moderate reliability, though non-obvious errors in morphosyntactic analysis require an expert linguist to catch. With no general-studies designation and no licensure mandate, and as a senior-standing terminal course rather than scaffolding for further required classes, the binding constraint is verification burden rather than institutional lock-in, landing the rating at Medium.

By 2031, capability trends toward faster task-time-horizon doubling make it likely that AI systems apply typological and theoretical frameworks to novel language data with meaningfully greater reliability, and adoption in linguistics research and teaching workflows should be more visible even though diffusion nationally still lags capability. The instrumental case for a student personally performing the core analytical task -- classifying an unfamiliar structure under a theoretical lens -- weakens as AI increasingly produces a first-pass analysis. What remains necessary is the trained judgment to catch a plausible-but-wrong typological claim, precisely the jagged-frontier concern about miscalibrated trust outside a system's competence zone. Because the course carries no general-studies designation and functions as a senior-level terminal rather than foundational course, no factor caps the rating institutionally, and base automatability growth pushes the rating to High, with real but bounded uncertainty about how quickly rigorous linguistic argumentation follows.

A decade out, under a central case of continued rapid capability growth, AI systems plausibly perform most routine typological and theoretical analysis of language data competently, leaving the human contribution concentrated in framing novel research questions, adjudicating between competing theoretical accounts, and verifying claims about under-documented languages where training data is thin and errors are hard to detect. That verification role is genuine but no longer the load-bearing instrumental reason a student must take the course to perform the analytical work itself. The wide-uncertainty caveat is substantial here: linguistic theory building is closer to the protected critical-thinking end of the task-exposure spectrum than routine writing, and a slower-diffusion scenario is plausible. Still, absent any general-studies or licensure floor holding the rating down, and given a terminal senior-level course with no foundational scaffolding function, the central case places the rating at High rather than assuming durable necessity.
LING 4060.d: Students focus on at least two different theoretical approaches to language in this course. First, students approach language through the lens of language universals and the typological classification of languages, which allows them to examine all levels of linguistic structure from languages all around the world. Students also study other theoretical approaches, at least one in depth, and use the terminology and analytical methodologies that they have learned in previous courses to explain new linguistic situations. Finally, students prepare for post-graduation success by developing employment-related materials.
